title: The Venetian Arsenal Builds a Galley in a Day
text:
The Arsenal of Venice was one of the largest industrial sites in pre-industrial Europe: a walled complex of shipyards, ropewalks, foundries and warehouses where thousands of state-employed workers, the arsenalotti, built and fitted out the Republic's war galleys. Dante had already used its boiling pitch and busy shipwrights as an image of hell's activity in the Inferno.

Its secret was organization. Hulls were built in large numbers from standardized parts and stored ready to be finished. In 1436 the Spanish traveler Pero Tafur described how, at the Arsenal's exit, a galley was towed along a channel past a row of windows, and from each window workers handed out what it needed: cordage, arms, oars, provisions. By the end of the line it was ready for sea, and he saw ten galleys fitted out this way in a matter of hours.

The most famous story comes from July 1574, when King Henry III of France visited Venice on his way home from Poland. According to Venetian accounts, the arsenalotti began assembling a galley from prepared parts when the king sat down to a banquet, and had it complete and launched before he rose from the table.

Whatever the exact timing, the Arsenal could produce and outfit war galleys at a pace no rival yard could match. In emergencies, such as the war leading up to Lepanto in 1571, it turned out dozens of galleys within months.
lesson: Speed comes from preparation and organization more than from heroic effort. Standard parts, clear stations and well-drilled people can do in hours what improvisation does in months.
people: The arsenalotti of Venice, Henry III of France, Pero Tafur
source: Frederic C. Lane, Venetian Ships and Shipbuilders of the Renaissance (1934); Pero Tafur, Andancas e viajes (c. 1454)
caveat: The galley built during a single banquet is a celebrated story whose exact timing is probably embellished.
